attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the Player sprite’s velocity y and acceleration y values so it jumps when the A button is pressed, then falls back to the ground?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What value should be set in the [set sprite vy] block, so that the Player sprite jumps when the A button is pressed?

❓ Should the vy value be a positive or negative number? Why?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡If the velocity y value is positive, it will make the sprite move down. If the velocity y value is negative, it will make the sprite move up.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by coding the Player sprite to jump onto tilemap platforms!


Add a [set sprite [x]] block underneath the Player sprite’s blocks in the [on start] container. Use the drop down to select [ay (acceleration y)]. Set the parameter to 600.


In the [on button pressed] container already in the editor, replace the <true> value in the [if then] conditional with an <is sprite hitting wall> value block. Select [bottom] as the direction the program should check for. Then, add another [set sprite [x]] block into the conditional and select [vy (velocity y)] from the drop down. 


Test out the program to decide what parameter should be used in the [set sprite vy (velocity y)] block, so that the sprite’s velocity y allows the Player sprite to jump onto a platform. 


Click ▶ to explore the tilemap by making the Player sprite jump onto different platforms!

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the Enemy sprites to [ghost through walls] so it can move past the platform walls?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the [set sprite ghost through walls] impact the Enemy sprite?

❓ How does randomness impact how the Enemy sprites fall on the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Prompt the ninja to consider game design and appearance when adding in each of these blocks. Why might they want Enemy sprites to be placed randomly across the top of the tilemap and fall at varying speeds? What would the game look like if the Enemy sprites were unable to move through walls?
steps.instructions:
Notice the code, already in the editor, that creates Enemy sprites at the top of the tilemap. Code the raindrops to fall from the top of the screen, creating an obstacle for the Player sprite to avoid!


Add a [set sprite [x]] block to the [on game update every ms] loop, below the Enemy sprite’s blocks. Select [vy (velocity y)] from the drop down, then drag a (pick random) value block into the parameter. Make the program select a random vy value for the Enemy sprite between 30 and 60, so that the Enemy sprites fall at different speeds.


Drag a [set sprite auto destroy] block below the [set sprite vy (velocity y)] block, and set it to [ghost through walls]. Set the toggle to <ON>, so that the Enemy sprites can move through the platform walls without causing an overlap event. 


Click ▶ to see Enemy sprites fall from the top of the tilemap! Notice what happens when the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite.

steps.hints: ❓Did you open Variables and click [Make a Variable] to create a new variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you think might happen by setting [invincible] to <false> at the start of the project, then changing it to <true> on overlap with the Food sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to think through how the true and false Booleans might be used in a project. These two Booleans can make it easier to keep track of certain game conditions and cause certain things to happen based on different events.
steps.instructions:
Protect the Player sprite from the Enemy sprites on overlap with a Food sprite!


Add a new variable to the [on start] container named invincible. Then, open Logic and drag a <false> Boolean into the parameter of the [set [invincible] to] block. This will set the invincible variable to “false” when the project starts. 


Duplicate the [set [invincible] to] block and place it at the top of the [on (Player) overlaps (Food)] container. Use the drop down to select <true>. This will change the invincible variable from “false” to “true” after the Player sprite has overlapped the umbrella sprite.

steps.hints: ❓Did you create a new variable and set it to the number of seconds the Player sprite will have invincibility for?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How long will the timer last when the [start countdown] block is run? How do you know?

❓ What else do you think the powerUp variable might be used for in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja of the connection between the [set [powerUp] to] block and the (powerUp) variable. The (powerUp) variable simply inputs the value of the powerUp variable in whichever parameter it takes. Consequently, the timer will last for 5 seconds when the [start countdown] block is run.
steps.instructions:
Make the Player sprite invincible to Enemy sprites for a short amount of time.


Add another variable to the [on start] container and name it powerUp. Type “5” in the bubble of the [set [powerUp] to] block. This will represent the number of seconds that the Player sprite has invincibility for.


Add a [start countdown] block into the bottom of the [on (Player) overlaps (Food)] container. Use a (powerUp) variable as the parameter in the [start countdown] block.


Click ▶ to see a 5 second countdown appear on the screen, after the Player sprite overlaps a Food sprite!

steps.hints: ❓Did you multiply the powerUp variable by 1000 so it is converted to milliseconds in the [set sprite lifespan] and [sprite start effect] blocks?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does the powerUp variable need to be multiplied by 1000 in the [set sprite lifespan] and [sprite start effect] blocks?

❓How long will the Food sprite’s lifespan and sprite effect last? How do you know?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice the units used in the [set powerUp to] block versus the [set sprite lifespan] and [sprite start effect] blocks. The [set powerUp to] block uses seconds, whereas the [set sprite lifespan] and [sprite start effect] blocks use milliseconds. As a result, the (0 x 0) operator is used to convert the variable value into milliseconds by multiplying the value by 1000.
steps.instructions:
Code the Food sprite to protect the Player sprite while invincible! 


Add a [set sprite [x]] block above the [start countdown] block in the [on (Player) overlaps (Food)] container. Drag an (otherSprite) bubble into the sprite name and select [lifespan] from the drop down.


Place a [sprite start effect] block underneath the [set sprite lifespan] block. Drag a (sprite) bubble into the sprite name and select an effect.


Open Math and add a (0 x 0) operator into the parameter of the [set sprite lifespan] block. Drag a (powerUp) variable into the left parameter and type “1000” in the right parameter. Duplicate the entire (0 x 0) operator and place it in the parameter of the [sprite start effect] block. The (0 x 0) operator converts the powerUp variable from seconds into milliseconds, which are used in the [set sprite lifespan] and [sprite start effect] blocks.


Click ▶ to overlap a Food sprite, then notice what happens while the Player sprite is invincible!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a <not> Boolean with the  (invincible) variable in the [if then] conditional?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What needs to be true, in order for the conditional to run?

❓ What is the <not> Boolean checking for in this example?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡In this example, the <not> Boolean is being used to check if the [invincible] variable is false. If the Player sprite does not have invincibility, then destroy the Enemy sprite and change life by -1.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The Player sprite still loses a life on overlap with an Enemy sprite, even when it’s invincible!


Open Logic and drag a <not> Boolean into the <true> value of the [if then] conditional in the [on (Player) overlaps (Enemy)] container. 


Then, drag an (invincible) variable into the parameter of the <not> Boolean. Now, the project only takes a life away on overlap with an Enemy sprite when the invincible variable is “false”. 


Click ▶ to see the number of lives remain the same on overlap with an Enemy sprite when the Player sprite is invincible!

steps.hints: ❓Did you change the Player sprite’s invincibility to <false>, then create a function to create a Food sprite in the [on start] and [on countdown end] containers?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓How do you create a new function?

❓What will happen once the countdown ends? Why is it important to reset the [invincible] variable back to <false>?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Prompt the ninja to consider why the [invincible] variable should be reset to <false>. Ask the ninja what would happen if the variable was not reset the next time the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite —would they remain invincible or lose a life?
steps.instructions:
Remove the Player sprite’s protection once the countdown ends! 


Drag out an [on countdown end] container and add a [set [invincible] to] block into it. Open Logic and add a <false> Boolean into the [set [invincible] to] block.


Instead of duplicating the Food sprite’s code to reset it once destroyed, create a new function named makeUmbrella. Drag the Food sprite’s blocks from the [on start] container into the [function makeUmbrella] container. Add [call makeUmbrella] blocks into the [on start] and [on countdown end] containers.


Click ▶ to see the Food sprite reappear on a random tile after the Player sprite’s invincibility has ended.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add [set score to] and [change score by] blocks into the correct containers?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution

Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the Player sprite earn a point in this game?

❓ What needs to be true, in order for the game to end in a win?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Walk the ninja through the logic of the score variable. In this example, each time the Player sprite avoids the Enemy sprite, as in either overlaps it with invincibility or does not overlap it at all, a point is added to the score.
steps.instructions:
Keep track of how many Enemy sprites are avoided, and end the game once a certain number is reached!


Add a [set score to] block into the [on start] container, below the [set life to] block, then add a [change score by] block into the [on sprite overlaps tile] container. 


Drag an [if then] conditional into the [on sprite overlaps tile] container and replace the <true> value with a <0=0> comparison block. Place a (score) variable into the left parameter and type a value into the right parameter with the number of points the Player sprite needs to win the game.


Place a [game over] block into the conditional and set the toggle to <WIN>.


Click ▶ to avoid the falling Enemy sprites and earn enough points to win the game!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add customizations to your project, such as dialog boxes, splash screens, or effects?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might help a user understand how to play the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Make the project more engaging by adding directions with a dialog box and frame, setting a background color, and including any sound or visual effects.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a 2D platformer project that uses Booleans to make different things happen when sprites overlap!

validationItems.text: Player sprite jumps up when the A button is pressed and the bottom of the sprite is touching a tilemap wall tile.
Enemy sprites fall from the top of the tilemap and ghost through walls.
Set the Player sprite’s invincibility with a variable.
Use a variable to control the invincibility countdown.
Invincibility effects last as long as the countdown.
Invincibility resets when the countdown ends.
Enemy sprites change life by -1 when the Player sprite is not invincible.
Game ends when the Player sprite avoids a specific number of Enemy sprites.
Game instructions are shared in a dialog box. Sound and visual effects are added to the game.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Green Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about Booleans and logic operators. Booleans can be useful to check if specific and/or multiple conditions have been met in a project. They can also be useful in 2D platformer projects to keep track of certain game conditions and to make something happen on certain tilemap events. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: It All Keeps Adding Up
badges.description: Use logic and math to make different things happen in a project.

badges.title: All or Nothing
badges.description: Check if two conditions are both true in a conditional statement.

badges.title: Fork in the Road
badges.description: Check if one of two conditions is true in a conditional statement.

badges.title: Nuh-Uh!
badges.description: Check for the negative, or opposite, of a variable’s current value.

badges.title: Yes/No Question
badges.description: Set a condition using the Boolean values true or false.

badges.title: Knowing Your Surroundings
badges.description: Check for the tile next to a sprite before making something happen in a project.

badges.title: Splat!
badges.description: Set a sprite to be destroyed whenever it touches a tilemap wall.

badges.title: Math Magician
badges.description: Perform a mathematical operation in a project’s code.
